content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by difficulties in social communication and interaction, as well as restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior and interests. While some individuals view autism as an integral part of their identity, others experience significant challenges and may seek treatment. Currently, no interventions exist that completely eliminate the features of autism. Acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter in the cholinergic system, plays a role in attention, novelty-seeking, and memory. Low levels of acetylcholine have been hypothesized to contribute to autism symptoms. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, such as donepezil, galantamine, and rivastigmine, work by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine. These drugs have slightly different mechanisms of action and bioavailability, which may result in varying levels of effectiveness and side effects. However, the impact of these medications on core autism features (social interaction, communication, and restricted/repetitive behaviors) and their potential adverse effects have not been thoroughly studied. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in addressing the core features of autism, as well as their effects on non-core features such as language, irritability, hyperactivity, and general health and functioning. A systematic search was conducted in November 2022 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as trial registries. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., galantamine, donepezil, or rivastigmine) administered orally or via transdermal patches, either as monotherapy or adjunct therapy, were included. Participants of any age with a clinical diagnosis of autism were eligible. Standard Cochrane methodologies were used, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Two RCTs, involving a total of 74 participants, were included in the review. One study was conducted in Iran, and the other in the United States (specific location unclear). Galantamine Plus Risperidone vs. Placebo Plus Risperidone One study compared the combination of galantamine and risperidone to placebo and risperidone in 40 children aged 4 to 12 years. Outcomes were measured using subscales of the Aberrant Behavior Checklist (ABC), where higher scores indicate greater impairment. The evidence, rated as very low certainty, suggested little to no difference between the two groups in social communication (mean difference [MD] -2.75, 95% confidence interval [CI] -5.88 to 0.38) or restricted and repetitive behaviors (MD -0.55, 95% CI -3.47 to 2.37) after the intervention. Overall autism features were not assessed. Adverse events were more frequent in the galantamine plus risperidone group (75%) compared to the placebo plus risperidone group (35%), with an odds ratio of 5.57 (95% CI 1.42 to 21.86). However, no serious adverse events were reported. Low-certainty evidence indicated a small improvement in irritability (MD -3.50, 95% CI -6.39 to -0.61) in the galantamine group. There was no evidence of a difference in hyperactivity (MD -5.20, 95% CI -10.51 to 0.11). General health and functioning were not assessed. Donepezil vs. Placebo The second study compared donepezil to placebo in 34 participants aged 8 to 17 years. Outcomes were measured using subscales of the Modified Version of the Real Life Rating Scale, where higher scores indicate greater impairment. Very low-certainty evidence showed no significant differences between the groups in overall autism features (MD 0.07, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.33), social communication (MD -0.02, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.30), or restricted and repetitive behaviors (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.35) after the intervention. Adverse events leading to study withdrawal were implied but not explicitly reported. The evidence was very uncertain regarding the effects of donepezil on secondary outcomes, including irritability (MD 1.08, 95% CI -0.41 to 2.57), hyperactivity (MD 2.60, 95% CI 0.50 to 4.70), and general health and functioning (MD 0.03, 95% CI -0.48 to 0.54). Across all analyses, the evidence was judged to be of very low certainty due to high risk of bias and serious imprecision, as the results were based on a single small study with wide confidence intervals. Adverse events were narratively reported for the study as a whole, rather than by treatment group. Authors' Conclusions The current evidence regarding the effectiveness of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors for improving outcomes in autistic individuals is limited and highly uncertain. There is a lack of evidence for their use in autistic adults, and the evidence for autistic children is inconclusive. Further research is needed to evaluate the clinical relevance of these medications for autistic individuals and their families. Several ongoing studies may provide additional insights in future updates of this review.
